title: Cross-Model Autograder Bias Audit Using Safety Evaluation Prompts

original_idea.title: Cross-Model Autograder Bias Audit Using Safety Evaluation Prompts
original_idea.problem: LLM judges used for safety evaluation show systematic family-bias -- they score outputs from the same model family higher. This inflates safety scores for models evaluated by their own family's judge.
original_idea.direction: Select 3 open-source judge models and have each grade the same set of 100-200 safety-relevant model outputs. Compute inter-judge agreement (Cohen's Kappa) and measure whether each judge systematically favors its own family. Visualize score distributions and report a 'judge bias score'.
original_idea.why_it_matters: Safety evaluation pipelines often use a single LLM judge. If that judge is biased, the entire evaluation is compromised. Documenting this for safety-specific prompts is more urgent than for general tasks.
original_idea.relevant_context: RAND's Judge Reliability Harness (2025) and the AISI Skewed Score framework both confirm judge unreliability. No study has focused specifically on family-bias in safety evaluations.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: documenting family bias in safety judges motivates cross-family evaluation protocols. Direct practical impact on how safety evaluations are conducted.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Running 3 models as judges on the same dataset and computing agreement statistics is straightforward. Uses standard Python and statistical libraries accessible to beginners with guidance.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped single experiment: 3 judges, one dataset, compute agreement metrics and bias scores. Very well-defined deliverable easily achievable within 30 hours.

novelty.reasoning: LLM-as-judge bias is well-studied. The paper 'Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge' identified 12 key bias types and proposed the CALM framework. BiasScope automates bias detection. Research confirms family bias exists (models favor outputs with lower perplexity under their own policy). However, the specific focus on safety evaluation prompts (rather than general tasks) has not been the subject of a dedicated study. The idea of computing a 'judge bias score' specifically for safety-relevant outputs and using Cohen's Kappa for inter-judge agreement in the safety domain provides partial novelty.
